Canva is restructuring 22% of its workforce.
Microsoft has offered voluntary exits to approximately 60,000 eligible employees.
Google has expanded voluntary buyouts across several countries.
And now Meta is reportedly offering voluntary exits too.

Four companies with different restructuring decisions, all while the technology industry continues investing heavily in AI.
There's a larger economic question behind this that I think deserves more attention.

Why are companies moving towards leaner teams while simultaneously investing heavily in AI?

Tasks that previously required hours of manual execution can now be completed with AI in minutes.
But cost-cutting doesn't begin and end with layoffs.
Businesses are also reconsidering agency contracts, consulting retainers, software subscriptions, outsourcing arrangements and other B2B partnerships.

If something can be done sufficiently well at a lower cost, there's a strong incentive to reconsider what you're paying for it.
For one company, that's a saving. For another, it's lost revenue.
An agency losing clients may reduce hiring. A software company losing subscriptions may cut vendor spending. Those vendors may then reconsider their own expenses.
And employees are part of this equation too.

The people and businesses whose costs companies are trying to eliminate are also customers elsewhere in the economy.

Of course, savings don't disappear. They can be reinvested, passed on through lower prices or used to create new opportunities.
But where those gains go, and how quickly they reach the wider economy, matters.
If enough businesses and individuals lose income faster than they can replace it, spending weakens. Lower demand encourages further cost-cutting.
And the cycle can reinforce itself.

For people waiting for the AI bubble to burst so they can return to working the way they did before, an investment bubble bursting doesn't mean the technology disappears.
Even if AI companies lose valuations or funding, businesses aren't necessarily going to abandon cheaper ways of operating that already work.

Which brings me to the contradiction I am thinking about.
An economy needs more than productive companies. It needs customers who can afford to buy what those companies produce.

I've explored both sides of this argument in a longer piece: Is AI a Bubble? What If It Bursts?

Follow along for more stories about the decisions, trade-offs, and execution problems behind running a business.

Every team wants an AI agent.

Few companies have a platform that makes agents safe, shared, and measurable.

That gap is hiring as AI Platform Engineer (also LLM Platform Engineer).

Not the person who demos a chatbot. The person who builds the shared layer so product teams stop reinventing production AI every sprint.

A tooling map for this role (five layers that keep showing up in India JDs):

1. Gateway
Route traffic to approved models. Rate limits, auth, policy. Teams call one endpoint — not 12 vendor keys scattered in Slack.

2. Serving
Inference that holds under load: containers/K8s, runtimes like vLLM or Triton when self-hosted, capacity and cost, not just "it works on my laptop."

3. Retrieval / context
Embeddings, hybrid search, citations, access-aware retrieval. The model only sees what it's allowed to see.

4. Tools / MCP
A managed catalog of tools agents can call — schemas, auth, approval flows, audit — so tool use is governed, not a free-for-all.

5. Observability + governance
Latency, tokens, cost, failures, SLOs. Security and responsible-AI controls enforced by the platform, not negotiated project by project.

These map to live Bengaluru postings as of Nov 7, 2026:
• GSK — AI Platform Engineer II (published Oct 28): LLM gateways, K8s/Terraform, MCP/agents, RAG, SLOs
• Ampere Computing — AI Platform Engineer: shared AI services, retrieval eval, MCP tool catalog, agent workflows
• Penguin Solutions — Sr. Software Engineer, AI Platform (posted Oct 10): model serving, RAG pipelines, vLLM/Triton, AI observability

Why it exists: pilots die without auth, budgets, reuse, and someone on-call for the platform.

Skills that keep repeating:
→ Python (+ Go/TS/Java helps)
→ K8s, Docker, CI/CD, IaC (Terraform)
→ LLM/API gateways (routing, rate limits, policy)
→ RAG + vector/search basics
→ MCP / tool contracts
→ Metrics, tracing, incident habits (OpenTelemetry-class)

Starter (laptop-sized "mini platform"):
Stand up an open-source LLM gateway (e.g. LiteLLM proxy) in front of 1–2 models. Add API keys + rate limits. Log latency, tokens, and estimated cost per request. Attach one tiny RAG path over a public doc set with citations. Write a one-page platform README: SLOs you'd promise, what you measure, what fails closed.

Show it: GitHub repo + a dashboard screenshot (or CSV) of p95 latency and $/1k requests. That language matches GSK/Ampere/Penguin better than another LangChain tutorial.

Do this today: list every place your org (or side project) hardcodes a model API key — and sketch one gateway that would replace them.

I hired my first teammate before either of us had anything that looked like a resume.

We were classmates at a college neither of us had chosen. He had decent English and no real plan. I had a handful of internship contracts and more work than I could do alone. Neither of us had a portfolio, a reference, or a single line on paper that would have gotten either of us an interview anywhere else.

I hired him anyway, on the only evidence that actually mattered: he showed up, he did the work, and he didn't need to be told twice.

That's still the entire filter I use now, at a very different scale. Credentials are useful as a signal, but they're a proxy for the thing I actually care about, which is whether someone takes ownership without being handed permission to.

The best people I've hired since have had wildly different backgrounds - some with impressive resumes, some with almost nothing on paper. The ones who worked out shared exactly one trait: they acted like owners before anyone gave them the title.

If that's how you operate and you're looking for a place where that gets noticed instead of overlooked, I'd genuinely like to hear from you.

As more agentic workflows take shape, we are getting a clearer view of their impact on the recruiter's day to day role. There has been plenty of debate, argument and resistance, but as pilots move into broader adoption, I think we are starting to define what I call the human hiring funnel.
This is the division between the critical human tasks and where agents carry the load. I see four areas.
The compliance tasks where laws governing AI in hiring require human involvement or supervision.
Requirements vary by state, country and use case. Agents can score matches, present candidates and make recommendations, but where human decision making is required, it must be meaningful. An auditable record should show the review, the reasoning and any overrides. Blind acceptance is no substitute for human judgement.
Hiring campaign set up is, in my view, best performed by humans, heavily assisted by AI. The job take on at the start of a campaign needs a human to human conversation between the hiring manager and recruiter. This sets the first social contract: agreed priorities, a timetable and the full brief driving the workflow. That conversation also gives the recruiter a chance to challenge the brief before an unrealistic requirement becomes a filter applied to every candidate.
This is where humans commit to follow up, preparation and actions. In my experience, commitments made to people carry more weight than commitments made to machines. The same applies to the final human to human commitment between a candidate and recruiter to turn up for an agreed interview.
The brief needed for a workflow needs to be deeper than a traditional hiring brief. The more information confirmed at this stage, including a ranking of the asks, the better the campaign should perform. Humans are supported by automated note taking and analysis, real time labour market insights, historical performance data and next step recommendations.
Humans providing the emergency stop or challenge button. Resistance to agentic workflows and AI screening and interviews can be reduced when candidates have the option to push the red button and speak to a human.
Candidates may prefer the agentic option at the top of the funnel for its speed and convenience, provided human help remains available. Match scores and assessments should also have a challenge option, with scores and rationale clearly explained. Where challenges are rare, that does not necessarily mean people agree with the machine.
Workflows need human set up, supervision and ongoing audit. Every campaign should be fine tuned after the intake meeting, with regular checks. Humans need the authority, time and information to question the workflow and change it. That includes checking who is being screened out, who reaches the shortlist, and whether results match the brief.
The agents bring the speed, reach, consistency and scale. The humans bring the relationship, the judgement and the adult in the room.
Peace Out,
Bill

I run a call center, and we test AI voice bots all the time. Here’s my honest take.

✅ Where AI voice bots win
They answer every call at 3 AM, on weekends and on holidays
Unlimited capacity, with no hiring and no training
Great for simple tasks: confirming appointments, reminders, FAQs, basic qualifying
Low cost per call at high volume
Every call is logged and summarized perfectly

❌ Where they fall short
They don’t truly listen. They respond to keywords, not emotions
Hesitation, sarcasm and “I need to talk to my wife” still trip them up
Customers hang up the moment they realize it’s a bot
No real rapport or trust, which is what closes deals
Objection handling is scripted, not human
One awkward AI call can damage a brand that took years to build

The truth: people buy from people.
A customer switching their internet, selling their house or signing a business contract wants to feel heard. That takes a human who can pause, read the room, crack a joke, and know when to push and when to back off.

What actually works in 2026: AI + humans together.
🤖 AI handles reminders, confirmations, data entry and first-touch screening
🧑‍💼 Humans handle conversations, objections, trust and the close
AI makes our closers faster. It doesn’t make them unnecessary.
So I’ll ask you:

👉 Would you buy something important from an AI voice bot?
Yes, no, or “depends”? Tell me in the comments. 👇

Think Texas AI compliance only applies to tech giants? That assumption is an operational trap.

Under Texas law (including TRAIGA / HB 149, Subtitle D), the rules govern anyone deploying or utilizing AI systems across commercial operations. The statutory standard does not require filing your employee handbook with the state for routine software use, but it does enforce strict accountability where business leaders least expect it: intentional discrimination safeguards (§ 552.056) and explicit biometric capture restrictions (§ 552.054(c)).

The immediate commercial danger is quietly unfolding inside your office every day. Staff members paste customer datasets, internal pricing sheets, and hiring notes into free AI platforms without enterprise-grade security.

Here are the critical operational exposures Texas owners face right now:

Strict Data Protection (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 521.052): Texas requires business operators to implement reasonable procedures to safeguard sensitive personal data. There is zero small-business carve-out.

Forfeiture of Trade Secret Status (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 134A): The moment proprietary formulas, client compilations, or financials are fed into an unshielded consumer AI platform, you risk legally forfeiting confidentiality and trade secret enforcement.

Personnel Action Exposure (Texas Labor Code Ch. 21): Relying on unvetted AI scoring to rank applicants or evaluate staff can introduce unlawful bias that exposes your company to avoidable liability.

Fortify your enterprise with the 4-Step Operational Guardrail:

Approved Enterprise Tools Only: Prohibit personal, free logins for company work; mandate commercial-tier solutions.

Strict Input Quarantine: Ban customer Social Security numbers, banking details, and proprietary trade secrets from prompt windows.

Mandatory Human Verification: Never issue customer commitments, contracts, or personnel determinations without human oversight.

Revocation of Connectors: Instantly terminate API access, drive integrations, and accounts the hour an employee departs.

🥊 Starting to feel like a boxer in today's job market, dodging scammers left and right!
It's gotten to the point where I'm questioning every recruiter who reaches out. I'm even starting to wonder if I've passed up a legitimate opportunity because I've become overly cautious.
Here are a few things I've learned along the way:
🚩 1. Check the email domain. Recruiter claiming to represent a company but emailing from Gmail or Yahoo? RED FLAG! I've had the same guy contact me from TWO different Gmail accounts.
🚩 2. Excessive flattery. Quoting your resume and telling you how perfect you are for a role before even speaking with you? RED FLAG!
🚩 3. Vague opportunities. Won't share details about the company or position but keeps pushing for your resume or a call? RED FLAG!
🚩 4. Moving off platforms. On Upwork, I've encountered obviously AI-generated messages (placeholders included!) followed by requests to schedule calls through Calendly before a contract exists, violating platform policies. RED FLAG!
🚩 5. Can't verify their identity. I actually had a "recruiter" tell me their LinkedIn account was undergoing "technical optimization" when I asked them to verify themselves. RED FLAG!
🚩 6. Artificial urgency. Pressuring you to send your resume immediately and discouraging verification because "the hiring team is moving quickly"? RED FLAG!
🚩 7. Inconsistent information. Job postings mentioning one company while advertising another, or recruiter details that don't match across platforms? RED FLAG!
The frustrating part is that not every red flag means it's a scam. But with so many out there, how do you avoid becoming overly suspicious and potentially missing a real opportunity?

Anyone else dealing with this? What red flags have I missed?

Meet actual humans.

The Wigwam Group is looking for an experienced Full-Stack Engineer to join our team, working on exciting projects at the intersection of AI, complex data and product development.
